slides.teach: Focus on the differences between the listed types and the clue words that distinguish them in exam questions.

course.learn: Security controls can be classified by what they do: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, or directive. The same technology can sometimes serve more than one function depending on how it is used.
course.why: Security+ scenarios often ask for the BEST control type based on purpose rather than the product name.
course.example: A visible camera can deter a person, while the recorded footage can also be used as a detective control after an event.
course.exam: Focus on the verb in the scenario: stop = preventive, discourage = deterrent, discover = detective, fix = corrective, alternative = compensating, instruct = directive.

breakdown.explanation: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage.
Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking.
Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation.
Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state.
A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended.
Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior.

course.learn: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage.
course.why: Prevention reduces the number of incidents defenders have to detect and clean up later, so it is usually the first layer of defense.
course.example: A firewall blocks an unauthorized inbound connection before it reaches a server. MFA can stop a stolen password from being enough to sign in.
course.exam: Look for words such as block, stop, prevent, deny, restrict, or before the incident. Do not confuse preventive controls with detective controls that only alert.

breakdown.explanation: Filter network traffic according to security rules, usually by source, destination, protocol, port, application, or context.
Use hard-to-guess credentials and limit what authenticated users can reach.
Protect readable data by converting it to ciphertext that requires an authorized key to recover.
Teach users how to recognize threats and follow secure behavior so human mistakes are less likely.

defs.definition: Transforms readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key so unauthorized parties cannot understand it.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Preventive and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Preventive controls are designed to stop a security event before it succeeds. They reduce the chance that an attacker, mistake, or unsafe action can reach the point of causing damage. Key ideas include: Firewalls; Strong passwords and access control; Data encryption; Security awareness training.

slides.title: Deterrent
slides.raw:
Deterrent
Security cameras and alarms
Intrusion detection systems
Security awareness posters and messages
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking.
course.why: A control can reduce risk even if it does not physically block an action. Visible monitoring and warning messages can change attacker behavior.
course.example: A clearly visible camera and a warning banner may cause someone to abandon an attempt even though neither one physically prevents the action.
course.exam: If the scenario emphasizes discouraging behavior rather than technically blocking it, deterrent is usually the best answer.

breakdown.explanation: Provide visible deterrence and evidence/notification when physical activity occurs.
Monitor traffic or activity for signs of attack and generate alerts; they do not normally block by themselves.
This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Security Control Types design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Deterrent and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Deterrent controls try to discourage a person from attempting an unwanted action. They work by increasing the perceived chance of being caught or the perceived cost of attacking. Key ideas include: Security cameras and alarms; Intrusion detection systems; Security awareness posters and messages.

slides.title: Detective
slides.raw:
Detective
Log monitoring
Vulnerability
assessments
Antivirus and antimalware software
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation.
course.why: You cannot respond to an incident you never notice. Detection shortens the time an attacker can remain active.
course.example: An IDS generates an alert after identifying malicious network behavior; log monitoring reveals repeated failed sign-ins.
course.exam: Look for alert, identify, monitor, discover, detect, log, or notify. IDS and SIEM are classic detective examples.

breakdown.explanation: Review events from systems and applications to detect suspicious behavior or failures.
Systematically identify and evaluate weaknesses so remediation can be prioritized.
Detect, block, quarantine, or remove malicious software on endpoints.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Detective and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Detective controls identify suspicious activity, policy violations, or evidence that an event has occurred. Their value is visibility: they tell defenders that something needs investigation. Key ideas include: Log monitoring; Vulnerability assessments; Antivirus and antimalware software.

slides.raw:
Corrective
Backups and

Incident

Software

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state.
course.why: Even strong preventive controls can fail. Corrective controls make recovery possible and limit the duration of an incident.
course.example: After ransomware is contained, an organization restores clean backups and patches the exploited vulnerability.
course.exam: Look for restore, remediate, recover, repair, remove, or after the incident.

breakdown.explanation: Maintain recoverable copies of data and documented recovery procedures so systems and operations can be restored after a failure or security incident.
Provide procedures for containing, eradicating, and recovering from security incidents to reduce damage and restore normal operations.
Applies updates that correct known vulnerabilities, security flaws, or software defects.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Corrective and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Corrective controls reduce damage and restore a system after a problem is discovered. They focus on fixing the condition or returning operations to a known-good state. Key ideas include: Backups and disaster; recovery plans; Incident response plans; Software patching.

slides.title: Compensating
slides.raw:
Compensating
Manual security reviews
Increased user training
Multi-factor authentication
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended.
course.why: Legacy systems, operational constraints, or cost can make an ideal control impossible. Security still needs another way to reduce the same risk.
course.example: A legacy application cannot support MFA, so access is restricted through a hardened jump server with strong authentication and monitoring.
course.exam: Compensating means alternative control—not a weaker synonym for preventive. The clue is usually that the normal control cannot be used.

breakdown.explanation: When an automated or preferred security control cannot be used, a person can manually review activity, configurations, or records to identify security issues.
Provides additional security education and guidance when technical controls are limited, helping reduce mistakes and risky user behavior.
Adds an additional layer of identity verification when another preferred access control cannot be implemented, helping reduce the risk of unauthorized access.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Compensating and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: A compensating control is an alternative safeguard used when the preferred or required control cannot be implemented exactly as intended. Key ideas include: Manual security reviews; Increased user training; Multi-factor authentication.

slides.title: Directive
slides.raw:
Directive
Security policies and procedures
Training materials and awareness campaigns
Risk assessments and compliance audits
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior.
course.why: Many security failures come from inconsistent human decisions. Clear direction creates repeatable expectations.
course.example: An acceptable-use policy tells employees which activities are prohibited on company systems.
course.exam: If the control is primarily an instruction, rule, policy, or required procedure, think directive.

breakdown.explanation: Document required security rules and repeatable steps for carrying them out.
Educate users about security policies, common threats, and expected behaviors to help reduce security risks and human error.
Evaluate risk and verify whether controls meet organizational, legal, or regulatory requirements.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Directive and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: Directive controls tell people what they are expected or required to do. Policies, procedures, standards, and mandatory training guide behavior. Key ideas include: Security policies and procedures; Training materials and awareness campaigns; Risk assessments and compliance audits.

slides.title: Confidentiality, Integrity, and Availability (CIA)
slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.
defs: Ensuring information is accessible only to authorized users and protected from unauthorized disclosure.
Ensuring authorized users can access systems and data when needed.
Ensuring data stays accurate, complete, and protected from unauthorized modification.
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability—the three foundational information-security objectives.

security_controls_layout.intro: Security controls can be classified in two different ways: by how they are implemented and by what they are trying to accomplish.

categories.name: Technical
categories.definition: Technology that directly protects systems or data.

categories.name: Managerial
categories.definition: Management decisions, policies, and planning that guide how the organization manages security and risk.

categories.name: Operational
categories.definition: People carrying out security procedures and day-to-day security activities.

categories.name: Physical
categories.definition: Things that physically protect people, buildings, equipment, or access to a location.

types.name: Preventive
types.definition: Stops a security problem before it happens.

types.name: Deterrent
types.definition: Discourages someone from attempting a security violation.

types.name: Detective
types.definition: Identifies or discovers a security problem or suspicious activity.

types.name: Corrective
types.definition: Fixes or reduces damage after a security problem occurs.

types.name: Compensating
types.definition: An alternative safeguard used when the preferred control cannot be implemented.
examples: Extra monitoring when MFA cannot be installed
Hardened jump server for a legacy system

types.name: Directive
types.definition: Tells people what they are required or expected to do.

exam_tip.type: Type = WHAT PURPOSE does it serve?

questions.q: A company configures a firewall to block unauthorized inbound traffic before it reaches an internal server. Which control type is BEST represented?
questions.explanation: Preventive. The firewall is stopping the unwanted traffic before the security event succeeds.

questions.q: An organization places a large sign outside a restricted facility stating, “24-hour video surveillance in use.” Which control type is the sign primarily providing?
questions.explanation: Deterrent. The sign is intended to discourage someone from attempting an unauthorized action.

questions.q: A security analyst receives an alert from an IDS after suspicious traffic is identified on the network. Which control type is the IDS functioning as?
questions.explanation: Detective. The IDS identifies suspicious activity and alerts defenders.

questions.q: After a ransomware incident is contained, administrators restore clean data from backups and return affected systems to normal operation. Which control type BEST describes this action?
questions.explanation: Corrective. The control is being used after the incident to restore systems and reduce damage.

questions.q: A legacy application cannot support the organization’s required MFA solution. The security team restricts access through a hardened jump server and adds additional monitoring. Which control type BEST describes the additional safeguards?
questions.explanation: Compensating. The preferred control cannot be implemented, so an alternative safeguard is used to reduce the same risk.

questions.q: An acceptable use policy tells employees which activities are prohibited on company-owned computers. Which control type is this?
questions.explanation: Directive. The policy tells users what they are required or prohibited from doing.

questions.q: A company requires employees to use multifactor authentication when accessing a cloud application. Which control category BEST describes MFA?
questions.explanation: Technical. MFA is implemented and enforced using technology.

questions.q: Senior leadership performs a formal risk assessment to determine which security risks should receive the highest priority. Which control category BEST describes the risk assessment?
questions.explanation: Managerial. Risk assessment is part of management planning and decision-making.

questions.q: A company deploys a firewall that automatically blocks unauthorized inbound connections. Which combination BEST classifies the control?
questions.explanation: The firewall is implemented through technology, making it technical, and it blocks the unwanted connection before it succeeds, making it preventive.

questions.q: A visible security camera is installed mainly to make would-be intruders reconsider entering a restricted area. Which combination BEST classifies the control?
questions.explanation: The camera is a physical security control, and in this scenario its main purpose is to discourage an intruder, making it deterrent.

questions.q: An IDS monitors network traffic and alerts an analyst when suspicious activity is found. Which combination BEST classifies the IDS in this scenario?
questions.explanation: An IDS is technology, so it is technical, and its role here is to detect and alert rather than block, so it is detective.

questions.q: An organization publishes a security policy requiring employees to follow approved password practices. Which combination BEST classifies the policy?
questions.explanation: A security policy is a managerial control, and because it tells employees what they are required to do, it is directive.

questions.q: Antivirus software finds malware on an endpoint and then removes the malicious files. Which control type BEST describes the removal action?
questions.explanation: The malware has already been found. Removing it is an action that fixes the problem, so that function is corrective.

classification_method.title: How to Classify Security Controls
classification_method.intro: Use this two-step method when a Security+ scenario asks you to classify a security control.

steps.title: Identify the TYPE
steps.question: What is the control trying to do?

classification_method.shortcut: First ask HOW? Then ask PURPOSE?
examples: Security policy telling employees what is required
Visible security camera intended to discourage intruders
Security camera footage reviewed after an incident

flashcards.title: Security control category vs. type
flashcards.answer: Category = HOW the control is implemented. Type = WHAT PURPOSE the control serves.
flashcards.exam: Use the two-step method: first ask HOW? Then ask PURPOSE?

flashcards.title: Technical security control
flashcards.answer: A control implemented through technology, hardware, or software.
flashcards.exam: Think firewall, MFA, encryption, IDS, and antivirus.

flashcards.title: Managerial security control
flashcards.answer: A control based on management decisions, policies, planning, risk, or governance.
flashcards.exam: Think policies, risk assessments, compliance requirements, and management decisions.

flashcards.title: Operational security control
flashcards.answer: A control carried out through people and day-to-day security processes.
flashcards.exam: Think training, incident response, manual reviews, and operational procedures.

flashcards.title: Physical security control
flashcards.answer: A control that physically protects people, facilities, or equipment.
flashcards.exam: Think locks, fences, guards, gates, cameras, and sensors.

flashcards.title: Control type memory shortcut
flashcards.answer: Preventive = stop; Deterrent = discourage; Detective = find; Corrective = fix; Compensating = Plan B; Directive = instruct.
flashcards.exam: Focus on the verb describing what the control is doing.

flashcards.title: Firewall classification
flashcards.answer: A firewall blocking unauthorized traffic is Technical + Preventive.
flashcards.exam: Technical tells you HOW it is implemented; Preventive tells you its purpose.

flashcards.title: IDS classification
flashcards.answer: An IDS that monitors and alerts is Technical + Detective.
flashcards.exam: IDS normally detects and alerts; an IPS can actively block.

flashcards.title: Security camera classification
flashcards.answer: A camera can be Physical + Deterrent when its visibility discourages intruders, or Physical + Detective when footage is used to identify activity.
flashcards.exam: The same control can have a different type depending on how the scenario says it is used.

flashcards.title: Antivirus classification
flashcards.answer: Antivirus can be Detective when it finds malware, Preventive when it blocks malware, or Corrective when it removes malware.
flashcards.exam: Do not memorize one permanent type for a tool; classify the function described in the scenario.
